title: 1500+ enemies at 60fps in a browser tab, and the bottlenecks Claude found that I'd been missing for months
author: CrisosDev
selftext:
Solo dev here. I've spent months on my survivors-like, Just Dying, wrestling with a single question: how many enemies can I have on screen without dropping below 60fps. I built a stress test to find the ceiling — it isn't meant to look good or be balanced, just to break.

The naive version died around 200.

And here's the part I actually wanted to write about, because it wasn't the part I expected: my problem was never that I couldn't optimize. It was that I couldn't tell *what* to optimize.

I spent weeks staring at flame charts in the profiler and getting nothing out of them. I could see the frames dropping. I couldn't see what was dropping them. I'd try something, gain 5%, look again, still understand nothing. That's the real dead end of working alone: you're not short on the ability to write code, you're short on someone to look at the data with.

That's where Claude came in. The workflow was almost stupidly simple: screenshots of the profiler and "tell me what I'm looking at." Since isolated screenshots didn't carry enough context, I built a separate debug profiling pass for the game itself — per-frame time broken down by system, active entity counters — and fed it that output too. With both together the conversation changed character. It stopped being "is this normal?" and became "this spike only shows up as enemy count rises and it doesn't scale with draw calls, so it isn't the renderer — look at per-entity cost."

Out of that came the four changes that actually moved the needle:

* **Enemies stopped being individual sprites.** They live in a particle container now, one batched draw call for the whole swarm; only bosses and elites keep a real sprite with their own animation rig. Biggest win by far. The cost: the swarm can't do anything a batched particle can't do, and every new visual effect has to be written twice, once per path.
* **Collision moved off the main thread.** Projectile physics, hit detection and damage over time all run in a web worker; the main thread just reads results. I kept the old version around as a fallback, which was a maintenance mistake — I now have two implementations of the same rules that have to agree with each other.
* **Spatial hashing** for neighbour queries, which is the obvious one. The non-obvious part: pooling the sets it returns. Allocating a fresh one per query per frame generated enough garbage to cause visible GC hitches. In a flame chart that doesn't look like your problem, it looks like the browser pausing for a moment. I'd spent months assuming exactly that. He found that one; alone I never do.
* **And the unglamorous stuff:** manual culling (Pixi 8 won't cull for you if you render directly), dirty flags everywhere so nothing recomputes what hasn't changed, and killing every per-frame allocation I could find.

Getting to the final number took a while, which was expected: every bottleneck you remove uncovers the next one and you have to measure again from scratch. But the time went into fixing, not guessing, and that's the whole difference.

End of the stress test: **1500+ enemies at a steady 60fps on my laptop**, up from 200.

I don't think I'd have gotten anywhere near that on my own. Not because it wrote code I can't write, but because it read the data that was sitting in front of me and that I couldn't interpret.

Where I'm stuck now: my machine is one data point. The browser build is the worst case — there's no native app underneath to absorb a bad frame — so I have no idea whether this holds up on a laptop with integrated graphics.

If you want to break it: [https://justdying.itch.io/just-dying](https://justdying.itch.io/just-dying) — runs in the tab, no download. There's a Steam demo too if you'd rather have a native build: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4646190/Just\_Dying/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4646190/Just_Dying/)

If the framerate falls apart on you, I want to hear about it. Your GPU, your browser and roughly when it happened is plenty.

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body:
Curious, did Claud use common game dev techniques around allocation optimization and cache friendliness like structs of arrays, typed arrays, pre allocated buffers, zero allocation hot loops, etc.? These are pretty standard things for high performance games but they aren’t common techniques in most JavaScript. Interestingly for my game, codex (even Astra ultra) failed to use any of these techniques without my prompting. It was however extremely good at profile and reducing render overhead like cutting draw calls.

I even was having it do full perf profiling passes on the entire codebase and it missed it. I had to specifically request it do a full optimization pass paying attention to this kind of stuff and track allocations and GC, which resulted in significant speed improvement to the game simulation and multiplayer netcode (anywhere from 2-6x faster depending on area). When I asked codex why it missed this stuff it said mostly because it’s a JS project and they are not common techniques represented in that training set, despite it having zero issues making all the changes when requested (the whole codebase perf pass was a one shot).

replies.author: CrisosDev
replies.body:
Yeah, interesting difference. I'm on Opus 5 and honestly it surprised me, it went after allocations and GC on its own, without me asking.  
  
Pooling the sets my spatial hash returns was its call, and that was the fix I'd spent months mistaking for "the browser just stutters sometimes". Structs-of-arrays and typed array buffers still never came up though, and I didn't ask either, so that might be the same JS training bias you're describing. Going to run an explicit pass asking for exactly that, curious if there's another 2x sitting there.   
  
Thanks for the pointer!

replies.author: SeasawPhilosopher
replies.body: Yeah if you have large numbers of entities to update, cache friendly code like struct of arrays can be pretty significant. I’d ask for that but also tell it to think in terms of systems style programming / high performance game programming rather than typical JS and write the code in a very cache friendly low/no allocation style even if it means sacrificing a bit of readability. When AI is writing the code, readability is less of a concern anyway, so these kind of optimizations make even more sense. Also if you’re doing multilayer over sockets make sure it uses binary data or encode/decode will kill perf.

replies.author: CrisosDev
replies.body:
Good call on the framing, I'll ask for it in those terms — systems-style, cache-friendly, zero allocations, readability be damned. On the netcode: this project doesn't have real-time multiplayer. Two players share a room but each one is instanced in their own map, and they send each other calamities through a deck system I built, kind of Clash Royale inspired, so there's no per-frame state to sync.

But I do have another project where exactly what you're describing applies: a multiplayer TD, up to 3 players, 2000+ entities, and it runs impressively well. I spent years in Unreal and all of this used to be a headache. Now it's a much shorter road.

The caveat I'd add though: this only works if you already have the knowledge base and a decent level of expertise. If you don't know what you're looking at, it's not going to solve your problems for you. You have to know enough to ask the right question, which is basically what your comment is an example of.
